project.title: All of Our Ancestors
project.subtitle: A deep-time atlas from LUCA to modern humans
project.aboutCaveat: These are representative lineage stages. Exemplar fossils are usually close relatives that illustrate what our actual ancestors may have resembled, not proven direct ancestors. The human lineage is bushy, not a clean ladder.

stages.name: LUCA
stages.fossils: No fossil; inferred from shared genes
stages.innovation: DNA/RNA/protein system, ribosomes, ATP metabolism, cellular life
stages.intro: LUCA is the inferred population from which all known life descends. It was not a modern bacterium or archaeon, but it already carried the core molecular machinery shared by cells today.

stages.name: Proto-eukaryote
stages.innovation: Mitochondrial endosymbiosis begins; larger, more complex cells
stages.intro: This stage represents the lineage near the origin of eukaryotic cells. A merger between an archaeal host and a bacterial partner set the stage for mitochondria and the larger, more compartmentalized cells that later animals would inherit.

stages.name: LECA
stages.fossils: No direct fossil; protosterol-biota as broad early-eukaryote signal
stages.innovation: Nucleus, mitochondria, cytoskeleton, membrane trafficking, likely sex
stages.intro: LECA was the common ancestor of living eukaryotes, including plants, fungi, protists, and animals. By this point the lineage likely had a nucleus, mitochondria, internal membranes, a cytoskeleton, and some form of sexual recombination.

stages.name: Opisthokont ancestor
stages.fossils: No secure fossil; living analogues: fungi/animals/choanoflagellates
stages.innovation: Rear flagellum, phagocytosis, cell-signaling toolkit
stages.intro: Opisthokonts are the broader branch that includes animals, fungi, and their microbial relatives. Our ancestry here was still single-celled, but it carried feeding, movement, and signaling traits that later helped make animal multicellularity possible.

stages.name: Choanoflagellate-like holozoan
stages.innovation: Collar cells, bacterial feeding, colony-forming potential
stages.intro: Choanoflagellates are not our ancestors, but they are close living relatives of animals and useful analogues for this stage. Their collar cells, bacterial feeding, and ability to form colonies help illustrate the toolkit near the animal transition.

stages.name: Stem animal, sponge-grade
stages.innovation: Stable multicellularity, cell adhesion, developmental gene regulation
stages.intro: The earliest animal-lineage organisms were probably simple, sponge-grade filter feeders. They mark a major shift from temporary cell clusters to durable multicellular bodies with specialized cells working together.

stages.name: Early eumetazoan-grade animal
stages.innovation: Tissues, nerves/muscles beginning, organized body axes
stages.intro: This stage sits near the origin of animals with organized tissues and body patterning. The fossil record is difficult here, but the lineage was moving toward coordinated cells, sensory systems, and more structured bodies.

stages.name: Urbilaterian-like worm
stages.innovation: Bilateral symmetry, front/back body plan, directed crawling, likely through-gut
stages.intro: Urbilaterian-like animals were small, wormlike organisms with a front end, back end, and left-right symmetry. That simple body plan opened the door to directed movement, burrowing, and the major animal branches alive today.

stages.name: Early deuterostome
stages.fossils: No perfect exemplar; Saccorhytus placement revised
stages.innovation: Deuterostome developmental pattern, pharyngeal-region innovations
stages.intro: Early deuterostomes were tiny animals near the branch that would eventually include echinoderms and chordates. Their importance is developmental: they sit on the side of animal evolution that later produced backboned animals.

stages.name: Early chordate
stages.innovation: Notochord, dorsal nerve cord, segmented muscles
stages.intro: Early chordates were small swimming animals with a notochord, dorsal nerve cord, and segmented muscles. They did not yet look like familiar vertebrates, but they established the basic body architecture our lineage still uses.

stages.name: Early vertebrate/craniate
stages.innovation: Head, paired eyes, early backbone/skull tissues, active swimming
stages.intro: Early vertebrate or craniate relatives added a distinct head, sensory organs, and stronger swimming machinery. These small Cambrian animals began the long vertebrate trend toward active movement and more complex nervous systems.

stages.name: Jawed vertebrate
stages.innovation: Jaws, teeth, paired appendage control, predatory feeding
stages.intro: Jawed vertebrates transformed feeding and locomotion. Jaws, teeth, and paired appendages made vertebrates more versatile predators and set up the later split between cartilaginous and bony fish lineages.

stages.name: Bony fish ancestor
stages.innovation: Bony internal skeleton, tooth/jaw refinements, lung/swim-bladder lineage
stages.intro: Bony fish ancestors carried a mineralized skeleton and refinements to the jaws and teeth. This is the branch that eventually produced ray-finned fishes on one side and the lobe-finned lineage leading toward tetrapods on the other.

stages.name: Lobe-finned fish
stages.innovation: Limb-like fin bones, stronger axial skeleton, air-breathing tendencies
stages.intro: Lobe-finned fishes had robust internal bones inside their fins, not just delicate fin rays. Those limb-like supports, along with air-breathing tendencies in related lineages, became important preadaptations for life in shallow water and on land.

stages.name: Fishapod
stages.innovation: Neck, flat skull, wrist-like fin bones, shallow-water ambush ecology
stages.intro: Fishapods such as Tiktaalik-like relatives lived in the ecological borderland between fish and early tetrapods. Flat heads, neck mobility, and wrist-like fin bones show a lineage experimenting with shallow-water movement before true limbs dominated.

stages.name: Early tetrapod
stages.innovation: Digits, limbs, weight-bearing experiments, new ear/neck mechanics
stages.intro: Early tetrapods had digits and limbs, though many still spent much of their lives in water. This stage marks the beginning of the vertebrate body plan that could push, prop, and eventually walk on land.

stages.name: Reptiliomorph
stages.innovation: More terrestrial skeleton, stronger ribs/limbs, reduced water dependence
stages.intro: Reptiliomorphs were increasingly terrestrial tetrapods on the stem leading toward amniotes. Their stronger limbs, ribs, and drier-land habits helped reduce dependence on aquatic environments.

stages.name: Early amniote
stages.innovation: Amniotic egg, claws, drier skin, fully terrestrial reproduction
stages.intro: Early amniotes solved one of the biggest problems of land life: reproduction away from water. The amniotic egg, tougher skin, and claws allowed this lineage to occupy drier habitats more fully.

stages.name: Basal synapsid
stages.innovation: Single temporal opening; stronger jaw muscles — mammal-side skull begins
stages.intro: Basal synapsids were early members of the mammal-side branch of amniotes. The key skull opening behind the eye gave jaw muscles more room, beginning a long trend toward powerful and specialized feeding.

stages.name: Sphenacodontian
stages.innovation: Larger canines, deeper skull, dominant terrestrial predator body plan
stages.intro: Sphenacodontians were larger predatory synapsids and close relatives of the line that led to therapsids. Dimetrodon is the famous side-branch example, useful for showing how mammal-line skulls and teeth were changing before mammals existed.

stages.name: Early therapsid
stages.innovation: More upright limbs, differentiated teeth, enlarged temporal fenestra
stages.intro: Early therapsids pushed synapsids toward more upright limbs, differentiated teeth, and more active lifestyles. They were still far from mammals, but many of the broad mammal-like trends became clearer here.

stages.name: Theriodont
stages.innovation: More active metabolism, canine specialization, secondary-palate trend
stages.intro: Theriodonts include the therapsid lineages closest to mammals. Features such as more specialized canines, changes to the palate, and increasingly active metabolism point toward the later cynodont condition.

stages.name: Basal cynodont
stages.innovation: Mammal-like teeth, secondary palate, larger jaw muscles, possible whisker/fur precursors
stages.intro: Basal cynodonts brought the mammal-like pattern into sharper focus. Their jaws, teeth, and possible whisker or fur precursors show a lineage becoming smaller, more active, and more precise in feeding.

stages.name: Triassic cynodont survivor
stages.innovation: Burrowing, small active body, survival through P–T aftermath
stages.intro: Triassic cynodont survivors lived through the aftermath of the Permian-Triassic extinction. Small, burrowing forms such as Thrinaxodon-like cousins illustrate how mammal-line animals persisted in a harsh, changing world.

stages.name: Advanced cynodont
stages.innovation: Better chewing, more upright gait, faster growth/metabolism
stages.intro: Advanced cynodonts improved chewing and posture while experimenting with a range of body sizes and diets. This stage sits close to the narrowing corridor that would eventually produce mammaliaforms.

stages.name: Probainognathian
stages.innovation: Mammal-like tooth replacement, jaw-joint experimentation, smaller body
stages.intro: Probainognathians were small, increasingly mammal-like cynodonts with important jaw and tooth changes. Their lineage experimented with the transition from reptile-style jaw joints toward the mammalian jaw and middle ear.

stages.name: Mammaliaform
stages.innovation: Dentary–squamosal jaw joint, middle-ear transition, hair, insectivory
stages.intro: Mammaliaforms such as Morganucodon-like relatives were tiny, likely nocturnal insect eaters. They show the emergence of the definitive mammal jaw joint and the hearing changes that helped mammals thrive in small-bodied niches.

stages.name: Early mammal-grade
stages.innovation: Larger braincase, sharper hearing, miniaturized nocturnal niche
stages.intro: Early mammal-grade animals refined the small, sharp-hearing, nocturnal body plan. Larger braincases, sensitive senses, and diverse teeth helped mammals exploit ecological spaces dominated elsewhere by dinosaurs.

stages.name: Therian stem
stages.innovation: Lineage toward placentals separates from marsupial line; arboreal/scansorial traits
stages.intro: The therian stem marks the broader lineage leading toward live-bearing mammals, including marsupials and placentals. Fossils such as Juramaia-like forms suggest small climbing animals near the split between major mammal branches.

stages.name: Early eutherian
stages.innovation: Placental-line anatomy, fur, climbing, tribosphenic molars
stages.intro: Early eutherians were close to the placental side of mammal evolution. They were small, furry, and probably agile, with teeth and limbs suited to climbing and insect-rich diets.

stages.name: Boreoeutherian ancestor
stages.fossils: No good body fossil; molecular node
stages.innovation: Placental diversification; primates + rodents/lagomorphs branch
stages.intro: The boreoeutherian ancestor is mostly known from genetic and comparative evidence rather than a clear body fossil. It represents the placental branch from which primates, rodents, carnivorans, bats, ungulates, and many other mammals later diversified.

stages.name: Primate stem
stages.innovation: Arboreal life, fruit/insect diet, grasping tendency after K–Pg
stages.intro: Primate-stem mammals appeared around the end-Cretaceous extinction and early Paleocene recovery. Purgatorius-like animals were small arboreal mammals, probably using grasping and flexible movement in tree-rich habitats.

stages.name: True primate
stages.innovation: Nails, grasping hands/feet, forward-facing eyes, leaping/climbing
stages.intro: True primates added a more recognizable suite of traits: grasping hands and feet, nails, and forward-facing eyes. These adaptations made sense in trees, where judging distance and holding branches mattered.

stages.name: Anthropoid
stages.innovation: Monkey/ape/human line: enhanced vision, shorter snout, enclosed eye sockets
stages.intro: Anthropoids are the monkey, ape, and human side of the primate tree. Shorter snouts, enhanced vision, and more enclosed eye sockets point toward the sensory world of later monkeys and apes.

stages.name: Catarrhine
stages.innovation: Old World monkey + ape line; two premolars; larger brain/body
stages.intro: Catarrhines are the Old World monkey and ape branch. This stage captures the lineage after it split from New World monkeys, with dental and body-size trends that would later lead toward apes.

stages.name: Early ape
stages.innovation: Tail loss, more mobile shoulders/back, ape-like climbing
stages.intro: Early apes lacked tails and had shoulders and backs suited for more varied climbing. They were not yet great apes or humans, but they mark the start of a body plan built around flexible movement in trees.

stages.name: Great-ape stem
stages.innovation: Larger-bodied apes, suspensory climbing, great-ape face/dentition trends
stages.intro: Great-ape-stem relatives were larger-bodied apes with suspensory climbing habits and changing faces and teeth. The exact fossil relationships are debated, but this is the neighborhood of the lineage leading toward African apes and humans.

stages.name: Hominin origin
stages.innovation: Smaller canines, possible early bipedality, human/chimp split zone
stages.intro: Hominin origins sit near the split between the human and chimpanzee lineages. Fossils from this interval are fragmentary and debated, but smaller canines and possible early bipedality hint at the beginning of the human branch.

stages.name: Early hominin mosaic
stages.innovation: Bipedal traits plus grasping big toe; glorious weird middle
stages.intro: Ardipithecus-like hominins show a mosaic of traits rather than a simple halfway form. They combined bipedal features with climbing adaptations, reminding us that early human evolution was not a straight march toward modern anatomy.

stages.name: Australopith biped
stages.innovation: Habitual bipedality, humanlike pelvis/knee, still small brain
stages.intro: Australopiths were habitual bipeds with small brains and bodies still adapted partly for climbing. They made walking on two legs a central part of the hominin lifestyle long before large brains evolved.

stages.name: Early Homo
stages.fossils: LD 350-1 jaw, H. habilis, H. rudolfensis
stages.innovation: Bigger brain trend, smaller teeth, tools/stone-flaking ecology
stages.intro: Early Homo marks a messy transition involving larger brains, smaller teeth, and more intensive tool-related behavior. The fossils do not form a neat ladder, but they show a lineage experimenting with new diets, hands, and cognition.

stages.name: Long-legged human
stages.fossils: Turkana Boy, Dmanisi fossils, Java fossils
stages.innovation: Humanlike body plan, endurance walking/running, dispersal beyond Africa
stages.intro: Homo erectus and ergaster-like humans had long legs, larger bodies, and endurance-oriented movement. They were the first human relatives to spread widely beyond Africa and maintained a successful body plan for a very long time.

stages.name: Middle Pleistocene Homo
stages.fossils: Sima de los Huesos, Kabwe, Bodo
stages.innovation: Large brains, big-game hunting, near sapiens–Neanderthal–Denisovan split
stages.intro: Middle Pleistocene Homo sits near the ancestry of Homo sapiens, Neanderthals, and Denisovans. Taxonomy is contested, but these populations had large brains, complex hunting, and growing cultural sophistication.

stages.name: Early Homo sapiens
stages.innovation: Modern face emerging, braincase becoming globular, complex tools
stages.intro: Early Homo sapiens populations show the emergence of the modern human face and a more globular braincase. They were part of a structured African population landscape rather than a single simple origin point.

stages.name: Recent modern humans
stages.fossils: Skhul/Qafzeh, later African and Eurasian fossils
stages.innovation: Symbolic culture, language-rich societies, global dispersal, cumulative tech
stages.intro: Recent modern humans carried Homo sapiens into a global species with symbolic culture, language-rich societies, and cumulative technology. This final stage connects the deep lineage story to the living people who inherit it today.
